claims.claim: EVTs were annotated as KRT7+, HLA-G+.
claims.source: CTBs were annotated as KRT7+, HLA-G-; EVTs as KRT7+, HLA-G+; immune cells as CD45+, VIM-; stromal cells as VIM+, CD45-; and the uterine epithelium by expression of EPCAM+, MUC1+, and MUC16+ (Figure 1c; Lee et al., 2016; McMaster et al., 1995; Vento-Tormo et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This describes the marker-based annotation of EVTs, supported by cited references and data in Figure 1c.

claims.claim: Immune cells were annotated as CD45+, VIM-.
claims.source: CTBs were annotated as KRT7+, HLA-G-; EVTs as KRT7+, HLA-G+; immune cells as CD45+, VIM-; stromal cells as VIM+, CD45-; and the uterine epithelium by expression of EPCAM+, MUC1+, and MUC16+ (Figure 1c; Lee et al., 2016; McMaster et al., 1995; Vento-Tormo et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This describes the marker-based annotation of immune cells, supported by cited references and data in Figure 1c.

claims.claim: Stromal cells were annotated as VIM+, CD45-.
claims.source: CTBs were annotated as KRT7+, HLA-G-; EVTs as KRT7+, HLA-G+; immune cells as CD45+, VIM-; stromal cells as VIM+, CD45-; and the uterine epithelium by expression of EPCAM+, MUC1+, and MUC16+ (Figure 1c; Lee et al., 2016; McMaster et al., 1995; Vento-Tormo et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This describes the marker-based annotation of stromal cells, supported by cited references and data in Figure 1c.

claims.claim: Uterine epithelium was annotated by expression of EPCAM+, MUC1+, and MUC16+.
claims.source: CTBs were annotated as KRT7+, HLA-G-; EVTs as KRT7+, HLA-G+; immune cells as CD45+, VIM-; stromal cells as VIM+, CD45-; and the uterine epithelium by expression of EPCAM+, MUC1+, and MUC16+ (Figure 1c; Lee et al., 2016; McMaster et al., 1995; Vento-Tormo et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This describes the marker-based annotation of uterine epithelium, supported by cited references and data in Figure 1c.

claims.claim: Cells expressing exclusive markers of disparate cell types were labelled as doublets and excluded from further analysis.
claims.source: Cells expressing exclusive markers of disparate cell types (co-expression of KRT7, HLA-G, HLA-A, VIM, ACTA2) were labelled as doublets and excluded from further analysis.
claims.evidence: This describes the quality control approach for identifying and removing doublets.

claims.claim: The complete dataset used for further analysis contained 50,496 cells that passed quality control.
claims.source: The complete dataset used for further analysis contained 50,496 cells that passed quality control (between 500 and 6500 unique genes, fewer than 15% mitochondrial reads, doublets removed) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a; McGinnis et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This reports the number of cells in the final dataset after quality control, with specific QC criteria listed.

claims.claim: Cells originating from the villous chorion numbered 25,367 and from the smooth chorion numbered 25,129.
claims.source: Cells originating from each region (VC – 25,367 and SC – 25,129) and each sample (7181–17,705 cells per sample) were well represented (Figure 1b; Figure 1—figure supplement 1b and c).
claims.evidence: This reports the distribution of cells by region in the dataset.

claims.claim: CTBs represented more than 60% of the cells in the integrated dataset.
claims.source: The number of cells in each broad cell type cluster demonstrated enrichment for CTBs, which represented more than 60% of the cells in the integrated dataset, as expected given the enrichment protocol (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
claims.evidence: This reports the proportion of CTBs in the dataset, which is consistent with the enrichment protocol used.

claims.claim: The sex of each fetus was inferred by assaying expression of XIST in trophoblast cells isolated from each sample.
claims.source: The sex of each fetus was inferred by assaying expression of XIST in trophoblast cells isolated from each sample (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a), which allowed the assignment of cell types to either fetal or maternal origin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
claims.evidence: This describes the method used to determine fetal sex and distinguish fetal from maternal cells.

claims.claim: 14,805 immune cells and 3,883 stromal cells were identified in the dataset.
claims.source: Even though there was enrichment for CTBs, we still identified 14,805 immune cells and 3883 stromal cells.
claims.evidence: This reports the number of immune and stromal cells captured despite the CTB enrichment protocol.

claims.claim: Immune and stromal cell subsets were reclustered individually and compared to previously published single cell analyses.
claims.source: We reclustered these immune and stromal cell subsets individually and compared them to previously published single cell analyses, allowing for the annotation of subtypes within each group (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a-d; Figure 1—figure supplement 4a-d; Figure 1—figure supplement 5a-c; Figure 1—figure supplement 7a-c; Vento-Tormo et al., 2018; Pique-Regi et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This describes the analysis approach for immune and stromal cells, including comparison to published datasets.

claims.claim: All immune clusters robustly expressed XIST in each sample, identifying them to be of maternal origin.
claims.source: All immune clusters robustly expressed Xist in each sample, identifying them to be of maternal origin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
claims.evidence: This uses XIST expression to determine the maternal origin of immune cells, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c.

claims.claim: Almost twofold more immune cells were recovered from the villous chorion than the smooth chorion.
claims.source: Almost twofold more immune cells were recovered from the VC than the SC, although it is possible that this change in proportion is an artifact of dissection and/or the CTB enrichment protocol (Figure 1—figure supplement 5d and e).
claims.evidence: This reports a difference in immune cell recovery between regions, with acknowledgment of potential technical artifacts.

claims.claim: The villous chorion contained a higher proportion of macrophages compared to the smooth chorion.
claims.source: Comparing the immune cell types identified in each region revealed a higher proportion of macrophages in the VC as compared to the SC, which contained a greater proportion of NK/T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5e; Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This reports differences in immune cell composition between regions, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5e.

claims.claim: The smooth chorion contained a greater proportion of NK/T cells compared to the villous chorion.
claims.source: Comparing the immune cell types identified in each region revealed a higher proportion of macrophages in the VC as compared to the SC, which contained a greater proportion of NK/T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5e; Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This reports differences in immune cell composition between regions, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5e.

claims.claim: The majority of stromal cells recovered originated from the smooth chorion (2941 compared to 942 from villous chorion).
claims.source: The majority of stromal cells recovered originated from the SC (2941 compared to 942 from VC).
claims.evidence: This reports the distribution of stromal cells by region.

claims.claim: Mesenchyme 1 and Mesenchyme 3 are largely smooth chorion-specific mesenchymal cell populations of fetal origin.
claims.source: These cells included lymphatic endothelium (Pique-Regi et al., 2019) and two largely SC-specific mesenchymal cell populations of fetal origin, Mesenchyme 1 and Mesenchyme 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 7c-e; Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
claims.evidence: This identifies specific stromal cell populations enriched in the SC, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 7 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claims.claim: Mesenchyme 1 and Mesenchyme 3 are marked by elevated expression of EGFL6, DLK1, and uniquely by expression of COL11A1.
claims.source: These two clusters are marked by elevated expression of EGFL6, DLK1, and uniquely by expression of COL11A1, which is observed only in the SC (Figure 1—figure supplement 7b and f ).
claims.evidence: This describes the marker genes for SC-specific mesenchymal populations, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 7b and f.

claims.claim: COL11A1 is expressed only in the smooth chorion.
claims.source: These two clusters are marked by elevated expression of EGFL6, DLK1, and uniquely by expression of COL11A1, which is observed only in the SC (Figure 1—figure supplement 7b and f ).
claims.evidence: This reports region-specific expression of COL11A1, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 7f.

claims.claim: HGF, WNT2, and RSPO3 were expressed in fetal stromal populations in both the villous chorion and smooth chorion.
claims.source: Interestingly, several canonical CTB support factors including HGF, WNT2, and RSPO3 were expressed in fetal stromal populations in both regions, suggesting shared requirements for WNT and MET signaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 7g).
claims.evidence: This reports expression of signaling factors in stromal cells from both regions, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 7g, with inference about signaling requirements.

claims.claim: The CTB subset is comprised of 29,668 cells.
claims.source: The CTB subset is comprised of 29,668 cells with similar representation and cell quality control metrics across all eight samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, b, and c).
claims.evidence: This reports the number of CTBs in the subclustered analysis.

claims.claim: Subclustering of CTBs identified 13 clusters including several CTB, EVT, and STB subtypes.
claims.source: This analysis identified 13 clusters including several CTB, EVT, and STB subtypes (Figure 2a; Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This reports the results of CTB subclustering, supported by data in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: Broad classes of trophoblast were annotated by established markers.
claims.source: Broad classes of trophoblast were annotated by established markers (STBs – CGA, CYP19A1, CSH1, CSH2; EVTs – HLA-G, DIO2; CTBs – PAGE4, PEG10, and no expression of EVT and STB markers) (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a; McMaster et al., 1995; Lee et al., 2016; Suryawanshi et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This describes the marker-based annotation of trophoblast subtypes, supported by cited references and data in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: Comparison to previously published cell types in the villous chorion and smooth chorion confirmed the identities of most clusters.
claims.source: Comparison to previously published cell types in the VC and SC confirmed the identities of most clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d-g; Vento-Tormo et al., 2018; Pique-Regi et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This describes validation of cluster identities by comparison to published datasets, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d-g.

claims.claim: Two cell clusters showed high expression of canonical phasic transcripts, including MKI67.
claims.source: Two cell clusters showed high expression of canonical phasic transcripts, including MKI67, with the S-phase cluster denoted by expression of PCNA and the G2/M-phase cluster by expression of TOP2A (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b; Tirosh et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This describes the identification of cycling cell populations based on cell cycle marker expression, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b and cited reference.

claims.claim: Both cycling populations share gene expression with all clusters of CTBs and were identified as actively cycling CTBs.
claims.source: Both populations share gene expression with all clusters of CTBs, and therefore, were identified as actively cycling CTBs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
claims.evidence: This describes the characterization of cycling cells based on shared gene expression with CTB clusters, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claims.claim: No STB or EVT markers were identified in the cycling clusters as was expected due to the requirement for cell cycle exit upon terminal differentiation to these lineages.
claims.source: No STB or EVT markers were identified in the cycling clusters as was expected due to the requirement for cell cycle exit upon terminal differentiation to these lineages (Lu et al., 2017; Genbacev et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This reports the absence of differentiation markers in cycling cells, which is consistent with established knowledge cited in the references.

claims.claim: CTBs separated into four clusters, CTB 1–4.
claims.source: CTBs separated into four clusters, CTB 1–4.
claims.evidence: This reports the number of CTB clusters identified in the analysis, shown in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: CTB 1 cells highly expressed PAGE4, PEG10, and CDH1.
claims.source: CTB 1 cells highly expressed PAGE4, PEG10, and CDH1 (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 4a), which have been shown to be canonical markers of villous CTB (Lee et al., 2016; Suryawanshi et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This reports marker gene expression for CTB 1, supported by data in multiple figures and cited references.

claims.claim: PAGE4, PEG10, and CDH1 have been shown to be canonical markers of villous CTB.
claims.source: CTB 1 cells highly expressed PAGE4, PEG10, and CDH1 (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 4a), which have been shown to be canonical markers of villous CTB (Lee et al., 2016; Suryawanshi et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a citation of previous studies establishing these markers for villous CTBs.

claims.claim: CTB 2–4 were more transcriptionally similar to each other than to CTB 1.
claims.source: Overall, CTB 2–4 were more transcriptionally similar to each other than to CTB 1, indicating a transcriptional program that was distinct from canonical villous CTBs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a and c).
claims.evidence: This reports the results of correlation analysis between CTB clusters, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a and c.

claims.claim: CTB 2–4 existed along a gradient of gene expression changes suggestive of various stages of a common differentiation pathway.
claims.source: CTB 2–4 existed along a gradient of gene expression changes suggestive of various stages of a common differentiation pathway.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the gene expression patterns observed in CTB 2–4, supported by the pseudotime analysis in Figure 3.

claims.claim: CTB 2 cells highly expressed CLU, CFD, and IFIT3, suggesting roles in responding to bacterial or viral infection through the innate arm of the immune system.
claims.source: CTB 2 cells highly expressed CLU, CFD, and IFIT3, suggesting roles in responding to bacterial or viral infection through the innate arm of the immune system (Thurman and Holers, 2006; Liu et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This reports marker gene expression for CTB 2 with inference about function based on cited references.

claims.claim: CTB 3 cells upregulated EGLN3 and SLC2A3, indicating an HIF-mediated response to hypoxia and a switch toward glucose metabolism.
claims.source: CTB 3 cells upregulated EGLN3 and SLC2A3, indicating an HIF-mediated response to hypoxia and a switch toward glucose metabolism, likely as an adaptation to the decreased oxygen levels in the largely avascular SC region (del Peso et al., 2003; Maxwell et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This reports marker gene expression for CTB 3 with inference about function based on cited references and the avascular nature of the SC.

claims.claim: CTB 4 specifically expressed several cytokeratins — KRT6A, KRT17, and KRT14, found in many epithelial barrier tissues and important for maintenance of integrity in response to mechanical stressors.
claims.source: Finally, CTB 4 specifically expressed several cytokeratins — KRT6A, KRT17, and KRT14, found in many epithelial barrier tissues and important for maintenance of integrity in response to mechanical stressors (Karantza, 2011; Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
claims.evidence: This reports marker gene expression for CTB 4 with inference about function based on cited reference and known roles of these keratins.

claims.claim: Previous analysis of the smooth chorion region at term using scRNA-seq identified fewer than 0.5% of trophoblasts as being CTB and did not identify a separate KRT6 expressing CTB population.
claims.source: Previous analysis of the SC region at term using scRNA-seq identified fewer than 0.5% of trophoblasts as being CTB and did not identify a separate KRT6 expressing CTB population (Pique-Regi et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a citation of findings from Pique-Regi et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Computational integration of the data from Pique-Regi et al., 2019, with the trophoblast subset confirmed CTB 3 and CTB 4 to be unique to this study.
claims.source: Computational integration of the data from Pique-Regi et al., 2019, with the trophoblast subset confirmed CTB 3 and CTB 4 to be unique to this study (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f and g ).
claims.evidence: This reports the results of computational integration with a published dataset, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f and g.

claims.claim: In the villous chorion samples, 53.8% of CTBs clustered in CTB 1 compared to 11.1% in the smooth chorion.
claims.source: In the VC samples, 53.8% of CTBs clustered in CTB 1 compared to 11.1% in the SC (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This reports quantitative differences in CTB cluster proportions between regions, supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: In the smooth chorion, 71.3% of CTBs were nearly equally distributed among CTB 2 (25.6%), CTB 3 (24.9%), and CTB 4 (20.8%).
claims.source: In contrast, the SC had a much larger proportion of the CTB 2–4 clusters. In this region, 71.3% of CTBs were nearly equally distributed among CTB 2 (25.6%), CTB 3 (24.9%), and CTB 4 (20.8%).
claims.evidence: This reports quantitative differences in CTB cluster proportions in the SC, supported by data in Figure 2d and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: In the villous chorion, only 24.1% of CTBs were found in CTB 2–4 clusters, with the majority in CTB 2 (16.1%).
claims.source: In the VC, only 24.1% of CTBs were found in the same clusters, with the majority in CTB 2 (16.1%).
claims.evidence: This reports quantitative differences in CTB cluster proportions in the VC, supported by data in Figure 2d and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: The contribution to cycling clusters was consistent across regions: 22.1% and 17.5% of CTBs in the villous chorion and smooth chorion, respectively.
claims.source: The contribution to cycling clusters was consistent across regions: 22.1% and 17.5% of CTBs in the VC and SC, respectively.
claims.evidence: This reports the proportion of cycling CTBs in each region, supported by data in Figure 2d and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: The relative proportions of CTB 1–4 in the villous chorion and smooth chorion were consistent across individual samples.
claims.source: The relative proportions of CTB 1–4 in the VC and SC were consistent across individual samples indicating that this difference was not driven by sample variability (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b-c).
claims.evidence: This reports consistency of findings across samples, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b-c.

claims.claim: Independent clustering analysis of villous chorion and smooth chorion cells identified the same populations as the integrated trophoblast subset.
claims.source: Furthermore, independent clustering analysis of VC and SC cells identified the same populations as the integrated trophoblast subset.
claims.evidence: This reports validation of the integrated analysis by independent clustering, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Independent clustering of the villous chorion did not identify CTB 4.

claims.evidence: This reports region-specific cell populations identified by independent clustering, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Independent clustering of the smooth chorion did not identify STB.
claims.source: Importantly, independent clustering of each region did not identify CTB 4 in the VC or STB in the SC, suggesting CTB 4 and STB to be specific to the SC and VC, respectively.
claims.evidence: This reports region-specific cell populations identified by independent clustering, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The small number of cells in the integrated dataset identified as villous chorion CTB 4 (173 cells) or smooth chorion STB (14 cells) may be in part an artifact of computational integration.
claims.source: The small number of cells in the integrated dataset identified as VC CTB 4 (173 cells) or SC STB (14 cells) may be in part an artifact of computational integration (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a-f).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the origin of small cell populations in the integrated dataset, supported by comparison to independent clustering results.

claims.claim: PAGE4 expression was highest in CTB 1 and decreased across CTB 2–4.
claims.source: At the mRNA level, PAGE4 expression was highest in CTB 1 and decreased across CTB 2–4 (Figure 2b and e).
claims.evidence: This reports gene expression patterns across CTB clusters, supported by data in Figure 2b and e.

claims.claim: In the villous chorion, the CTB monolayer between the fetal stromal villous core and the overlying STB layer showed strong PAGE4 immunoreactivity, which diminished upon differentiation to EVT.
claims.source: In the VC, the CTB monolayer between the fetal stromal villous core and the overlying STB layer showed strong PAGE4 immunoreactivity, which diminished upon differentiation to EVT (Figure 2f - left).
claims.evidence: This reports immunofluorescence localization of PAGE4 protein, supported by data in Figure 2f.

claims.claim: PAGE4 mRNA and protein expression matched that of known villous CTB marker CDH1.
claims.source: PAGE4 mRNA and protein expression matched that of known villous CTB marker CDH1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4a and b; Genbacev et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This reports concordance between PAGE4 and CDH1 expression, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4a and b and cited reference.

claims.claim: In the smooth chorion, the PAGE4 signal was strong in the epithelial layer directly adjacent to the fetal stroma and then decreased in cells distant from the basal layer.
claims.source: In the SC, the PAGE4 signal was strong in the epithelial layer directly adjacent to the fetal stroma and then decreased in cells distant from the basal layer, again matching CDH1 (Figure 2f – right, Figure 2—figure supplement 4b – right).
claims.evidence: This reports immunofluorescence localization of PAGE4 protein in the SC, supported by data in Figure 2f and Figure 2—figure supplement 4b.

claims.claim: Both PAGE4 RNA expression and protein localization were consistent with CTB 1 cells existing in both chorionic regions and occupying a similar niche.
claims.source: Both RNA expression and protein localization were consistent with CTB 1 cells existing in both chorionic regions and occupying a similar niche.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the PAGE4 expression and localization data presented in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Cells occupying the upper layers of smooth chorion epithelium showed a strong KRT6 signal, a pattern opposite to CDH1.
claims.source: Cells occupying the upper layers of SC epithelium showed a strong KRT6 signal, a pattern opposite to CDH1 (Figure 2h and i – right).

claims.claim: Rare decidual resident KRT6 positive cells were identified in the villous chorion region.

claims.claim: KRT6 isoforms, KRT6B and KRT6C, were not expressed in trophoblasts.

claims.claim: KRT6A transcript and protein are highly specific markers of a CTB population found only in the smooth chorion.

claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the expression and localization data for KRT6A presented in Figure 2 and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: RNA velocity analysis was performed to predict the relationships between cells based on the proportion of exonic and intronic reads.

claims.claim: Cells at the boundary of the CTB 1 cluster showed differentiation vectors of high magnitude toward STB Precursors and upregulated canonical drivers of STB differentiation and fusion (ERVW-1 and ERVFRD-1).
claims.source: Cells at the boundary of the CTB 1 cluster showed differentiation vectors of high magnitude toward STB Precursors and upregulated canonical drivers of STB differentiation and fusion (ERVW-1 and ERVFRD-1).
claims.evidence: This reports the results of RNA velocity analysis showing STB differentiation trajectory, supported by data in Figure 3a and gene expression data.

claims.claim: STB Precursor cells expressed transcription factors (GCM1 and HOPX) and hormones (CSH1) necessary for STB function.
claims.source: These cells also expressed transcription factors (GCM1 and HOPX) and hormones (CSH1) necessary for STB function (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a; Baczyk et al., 2009; Mi, 2000; Blaise et al., 2003; Yabe et al., 2016).

claims.claim: In the smooth chorion, CTB 1 cells showed strong directionality and magnitude toward CTB 2–4.
claims.source: In the SC, CTB 1 cells once again were identified as the root for differentiation. However, CTB 1 cells showed strong directionality and magnitude toward CTB 2–4 (Figure 3b).
claims.evidence: This reports the results of RNA velocity analysis for SC cells, supported by data in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: All cells in CTB 1–4 clusters displayed uniform directionality indicating a robust differentiation trajectory ending at CTB 4.
claims.source: All cells in CTB 1–4 clusters displayed uniform directionality indicating a robust differentiation trajectory ending at CTB 4.
claims.evidence: This reports the results of RNA velocity analysis showing the SC-CTB differentiation trajectory, supported by data in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: High levels of transcriptional similarity between CTB 2 and 4 compared to CTB 1 suggested CTB 2 and CTB 3 are intermediate states between CTB 1 and CTB 4.
claims.source: High levels of transcriptional similarity between CTB 2 and 4 compared to CTB 1 suggested CTB 2 and CTB 3 are intermediate states between CTB 1 and CTB 4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on correlation analysis, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claims.claim: Mitotic KRT6+ cells were identified, showing that differentiation to SC-CTB does not require cell cycle exit, unlike STBs and EVTs.
claims.source: Mitotic KRT6+ cells were identified, and while the interaction between the cell cycle and differentiation of SC-CTBs remains unclear, these data show that differentiation to SC-CTB does not require cell cycle exit, unlike STBs and EVTs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
claims.evidence: This reports the observation of proliferating SC-CTBs, supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, with inference about cell cycle requirements.

claims.claim: In the smooth chorion, no velocity vectors with directionality toward the STB lineage from the CTB clusters were observed.

claims.evidence: This reports the absence of STB differentiation trajectory in SC samples, supported by RNA velocity analysis in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: The smaller number of STB precursors (460 cells) and STBs (14 cells) in the smooth chorion exhibited reduced expression of STB canonical markers such as ERVFRD-1 and GCM1, and notably, a near absence of ERVW-1.
claims.source: Further, the smaller number of STB precursors (460 cells) and STBs (14 cells) exhibited reduced expression of STB canonical markers such as ERVFRD-1 and GCM1, and notably, a near absence of ERVW-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: This reports gene expression differences in the small STB population in the SC, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claims.claim: STB precursors and STBs in the smooth chorion may be associated with ghost villi.
claims.source: These cells may be associated with ghost villi (Benirschke et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the origin of the small STB population in the SC, based on cited reference.

claims.claim: Pseudotemporal modeling identified genes that were correlated with progression from CTB 1–4 in the smooth chorion.
claims.source: To identify the genes that were correlated with progression from CTB 1–4 in the SC, we used the velocity vector predictions to construct a pseudotemporal model of differentiation.
claims.evidence: This describes the computational approach used to identify genes associated with SC-CTB differentiation.

claims.claim: EGFR was expressed throughout all four CTB populations in both the villous chorion and smooth chorion.
claims.source: Genes that were highly expressed at the start of the pseudotemporal differentiation included pan-trophoblast factors such as EGFR, which was expressed throughout all four CTB populations in both the VC and SC.
claims.evidence: This reports gene expression patterns across CTB populations, supported by data in Figure 3c-d.

claims.claim: Progression along the pseudotime trajectory identified regulators of cell fate and function, including the transcription factor KLF4 and extracellular matrix components COL5A1 and LAMA3, all demonstrating smooth chorion-specific expression.
claims.source: Progression along the pseudotime trajectory identified regulators of cell fate and function, including the transcription factor KLF4 and extracellular matrix (ECM) components COL5A1 and LAMA3 (Figure 3c–d); all demonstrated SC-specific expression.
claims.evidence: This reports genes identified by pseudotime analysis as associated with SC-CTB differentiation, supported by data in Figure 3c-d.

claims.claim: Elevated expression of ECM transcripts (COL4A2, FN1) and transcription factors responsive to cell contact and mechanical stress (HES1, YAP1) were coordinately upregulated, potentially highlighting the effects of the extracellular environment on fate specification.
claims.source: Elevated expression of ECM transcripts (COL4A2, FN1) and transcription factors responsive to cell contact and mechanical stress (HES1, YAP1) were coordinately upregulated, potentially highlighting the effects of the extracellular environment on fate specification (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: This reports coordinated gene expression changes with speculation about their functional significance, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claims.claim: CellPhoneDB was used to predict receptor-ligand interactions between CTB clusters within each region to identify differential signaling events.
claims.source: To identify differential signaling events that might regulate alternative paths of differentiation in the VC and SC, we used CellPhoneDB to predict receptor-ligand interactions between CTB clusters within each region (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a-b; Efremova et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This describes the computational approach used to identify cell-cell signaling interactions, citing the method.

claims.claim: CellPhoneDB analysis identified BMP, Notch, and Ephrin signaling events specific to the smooth chorion region.
claims.source: This analysis identified BMP, Notch, and Ephrin signaling events specific to the SC region, which may help to determine cell fate and/or cell sorting within the SC trophoblast epithelium (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
claims.evidence: This reports the results of CellPhoneDB analysis with speculation about functional significance, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b.

claims.claim: SC-CTBs originate from CTB 1 progenitors common to both the villous chorion and smooth chorion.

claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNA velocity and pseudotime analyses presented in Figure 3.

claims.claim: In the smooth chorion, instead of upregulating syncytialization factors such as GCM1 and ERVFRD-1, CTB 1 progenitors upregulate transcription factors such as KLF4, YAP1, and HES1.
claims.source: In the SC, instead of upregulating syncytialization factors such as GCM1 and ERVFRD-1, CTB 1 progenitors upregulate transcription factors such as KLF4, YAP1, and HES1, which drive an epithelial cell fate in other contexts (Segre et al., 1999; Harvey et al., 2013; Rock et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This reports differential gene expression between VC and SC CTB differentiation trajectories, supported by data in Figure 3 and cited references about the functions of these transcription factors.

claims.claim: Gene ontology analysis was performed to understand the physiological functions of the smooth chorion trophoblast clusters.
claims.source: Next, we sought a better understanding of the physiological functions of the SC trophoblast clusters. We performed gene ontology analysis as a summary of functional processes (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Yu et al., 2012).

claims.claim: In CTB 1, gene ontology identified enrichment for WNT signaling, epithelial morphogenesis, and membrane transport.

claims.evidence: This reports the results of gene ontology analysis for CTB 1, supported by data in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Non-phosphorylated CTNNB1 (np-CTNNB1) was localized to the most basal epithelial layer nearest to the stroma in both the villous chorion and smooth chorion regions.
claims.source: We validated the activity of WNT signaling and the location of these cells by immunolocalization of non-phosphorylated CTNNB1 (np-CTNNB1). Staining was localized to the most basal epithelial layer nearest to the stroma in both the VC and SC regions (Figure 4b), matching expression of the CTB 1 marker CDH1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
claims.evidence: This reports immunofluorescence localization of np-CTNNB1, supported by data in Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claims.claim: WNT signaling has an important role in the maintenance of villous CTBs in vivo and in the derivation and culture of self-renewing human trophoblast stem cells.
claims.source: WNT signaling has an important role in the maintenance of villous CTBs in vivo and in the derivation and culture of self-renewing human trophoblast stem cells (Knöfler et al., 2019; Haider et al., 2018; Okae et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge, supported by cited references.

claims.claim: A similar percentage of KI67+ CTB 1 cells was observed in both the villous chorion and smooth chorion, suggesting similar proliferative capacity across regions.
claims.source: We investigated proliferation of np-CTNNB1 expressing cells in both regions using KI67 as a mitotic marker. This revealed a similar percentage of KI67+ CTB 1 cells, suggesting similar proliferative capacity across regions (Figure 4b and c).
claims.evidence: This reports quantification of proliferating CTB 1 cells, supported by data in Figure 4b and c.

claims.claim: Gene ontology identified an enrichment for oxidative phosphorylation and epithelial signaling cues in villous chorion CTB 1 cells.
claims.source: We next analyzed regional differences within CTB 1. Gene ontology identified an enrichment for oxidative phosphorylation and epithelial signaling cues in VC CTB 1 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b).
claims.evidence: This reports the results of gene ontology analysis comparing CTB 1 between regions, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b.

claims.claim: Smooth chorion CTB 1 cells displayed elevated levels of hypoxia response genes.
claims.source: This is in direct contrast to SC CTB 1 cells that displayed elevated levels of hypoxia response genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b-c).
claims.evidence: This reports differential gene expression in SC CTB 1 cells, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b-c.

claims.claim: KLF4 showed greater expression in CTB 1 in the smooth chorion compared to the villous chorion.
claims.source: KLF4 was identified in the RNA velocity analysis as gaining expression from CTB 1–4, but also showed greater expression in CTB 1 in the SC compared to the VC (Figure 3d).
claims.evidence: This reports differential KLF4 expression between regions, supported by data in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: KLF4 protein often co-localized to CTB 1 in the smooth chorion, but was only observed in rare cells in the villous chorion.
claims.source: In accordance with the mRNA expression data, KLF4 protein often co-localized to CTB 1 in the SC, but was only observed in rare cells in the VC (Figure 4d).
claims.evidence: This reports immunofluorescence localization of KLF4 protein, supported by data in Figure 4d.

claims.claim: CTB 4 gene ontology analysis showed greatest enrichment for cell junction and cell substrate adhesion genes.
claims.source: CTB 4 ontological analysis strongly supported important roles for these cells in the formation of a protective barrier. The greatest enrichment was for cell junction and cell substrate adhesion genes that included numerous integrin and laminin subunits as well as junctional proteins PATJ, DSP, and JUP.
claims.evidence: This reports the results of gene ontology analysis for CTB 4, supported by data in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: CTB 4 gene ontology showed enrichment for both skin and epidermal development.
claims.source: An enrichment for both skin and epidermal development correlated with upregulation of the ECM and junctional transcripts.
claims.evidence: This reports the results of gene ontology analysis for CTB 4, supported by data in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: Skin and epidermal development gene ontology categories included many cytokeratins (KRT6A, 7, 8, 14, 17, 18, and 19) and transcription factors (KLF4, YAP1) required for epidermal identity and maintenance.
claims.source: These categories included many cytokeratins (KRT6A, 7, 8, 14, 17, 18, and 19) and transcription factors (KLF4, YAP1) required for epidermal identity and maintenance (Segre et al., 1999; Schlegelmilch et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This reports genes in the epidermal development ontology category with citation of their known functions.

claims.claim: The organization of the smooth chorion is reminiscent of stratified epidermal cells of the skin, with progenitors adherent to the basal lamina and more differentiated cells forming the upper layers.
claims.source: The organization of the SC is reminiscent of stratified epidermal cells of the skin, with progenitors adherent to the basal lamina and more differentiated cells progeny forming the upper layers.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial organization observed in immunofluorescence images (Figure 2, Figure 4) and the gene expression patterns.

claims.claim: Cytokeratins 7, 8, and 18 were expressed in all trophoblast regardless of region.
claims.source: Cytokeratins 7, 8, and 18 were expressed in all trophoblast regardless of region (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a), but cytokeratin 6A, 14, and 17 displayed SC-specific expression that increased with differentiation toward CTB 4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3b).
claims.evidence: This reports cytokeratin expression patterns across trophoblast populations, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3a.

claims.claim: Cytokeratin 6A, 14, and 17 displayed smooth chorion-specific expression that increased with differentiation toward CTB 4.
claims.source: Cytokeratins 7, 8, and 18 were expressed in all trophoblast regardless of region (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a), but cytokeratin 6A, 14, and 17 displayed SC-specific expression that increased with differentiation toward CTB 4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3b).
claims.evidence: This reports region-specific cytokeratin expression patterns, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3b.

claims.claim: Immunofluorescence localization confirmed expression of KRT14 as specific to the CTBs in the smooth chorion and inclusive of all KRT6 expressing cells.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence localization confirmed expression of KRT14 as specific to the CTBs in the SC and inclusive of all KRT6 expressing cells (Figure 4e).
claims.evidence: This reports immunofluorescence validation of KRT14 expression, supported by data in Figure 4e.

claims.claim: Cytokeratin expression in smooth chorion CTBs begins with CTB 1 (KRT7, KRT8, KRT18), increases in CTB 2–3 (KRT14, KRT17), and culminates in CTB 4 (KRT6A).
claims.source: These data support a model of accumulated cytokeratin expression that begins with CTB 1 (KRT7, KRT8, KRT18), increases in CTB 2–3 (KRT14, KRT17), and culminates in CTB 4 (KRT6A).
claims.evidence: This is a model proposed based on the cytokeratin expression patterns observed in the data (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).

claims.claim: An enrichment for genes involved in antiviral response was identified in SC-CTBs.
claims.source: Beyond forming a physical barrier, important chorionic functions include protection from bacterial and viral infections. We identified an enrichment for genes involved in antiviral response in SC-CTBs, and in SC cells more broadly.
claims.evidence: This reports the results of gene ontology analysis, supported by data in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: IFITM3, a restriction factor preventing entry of viruses into cells, is highly expressed in CTBs from the smooth chorion compared to the villous chorion.
claims.source: For example, IFITM3, a restriction factor preventing entry of viruses into cells, is highly expressed in CTBs from the SC compared to the VC (Figure 4—figure supplement 4; Bailey et al., 2014; Spence et al., 2019).

claims.claim: IFITM proteins have been reported to inhibit syncytialization.

claims.evidence: This is a citation of a previous study's findings with speculation about the function of IFITM3 in the SC.

claims.claim: IFITM3 may function to block differentiation of CTBs into STBs in the smooth chorion.
claims.source: IFITM proteins have also been reported to inhibit syncytialization (Buchrieser et al., 2019), suggesting IFITM3 may also function to block differentiation of CTBs into STBs in the SC.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the cited function of IFITM proteins and the expression pattern of IFITM3 in the SC.

claims.claim: EVTs are the invasive trophoblasts of the placenta.
claims.source: EVTs are the invasive trophoblasts of the placenta (Knöfler et al., 2019; Turco et al., 2018; Red-Horse et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge, supported by cited references.

claims.claim: EVTs of the villous chorion migrate away from the villi, invade the decidua, and replace the endothelial lining of the uterine arteries.
claims.source: While the EVTs of the VC migrate away from the villi, invade the decidua, and replace the endothelial lining of the uterine arteries, the EVTs of the SC adhere to the decidua and do not home to the maternal vasculature (Genbacev et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about VC EVT behavior, supported by the cited reference.

claims.claim: EVTs of the smooth chorion adhere to the decidua and do not home to the maternal vasculature.
claims.source: While the EVTs of the VC migrate away from the villi, invade the decidua, and replace the endothelial lining of the uterine arteries, the EVTs of the SC adhere to the decidua and do not home to the maternal vasculature (Genbacev et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about SC EVT behavior, supported by the cited reference and confirmed by immunofluorescence data in this study (Figure 5b).

claims.claim: Expression of HLA-G was similarly abundant among cells isolated from both the villous chorion and smooth chorion regions.
claims.source: Expression of the canonical marker of EVTs, HLA-G, was similarly abundant among the cells isolated from both chorionic regions (Figure 5a and b).
claims.evidence: This reports HLA-G expression in EVTs from both regions, supported by data in Figure 5a and b.

claims.claim: A greater number (villous chorion – 6572; smooth chorion – 5021) and larger proportion (villous chorion – 46.83%; smooth chorion – 32.12%) of CTBs from the villous chorion expressed HLA-G as compared to the smooth chorion.
claims.source: A greater number (VC – 6572; SC – 5021) and larger proportion (VC – 46.83%; SC – 32.12%) of CTBs from the VC expressed HLA-G as compared to the analogous population from the SC (Figure 5c).
claims.evidence: This reports quantitative differences in EVT numbers and proportions between regions, supported by data in Figure 5c.

claims.claim: Immunolocalization of HLA-G showed strong staining of cells in both the villous chorion and smooth chorion.
claims.source: Consistent with the transcript expression data, immunolocalization of HLA-G showed strong staining of cells in both the VC and SC.
claims.evidence: This reports immunofluorescence validation of HLA-G expression, supported by data in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: Villous chorion derived HLA-G positive cells were found deep in the maternal decidua.

claims.evidence: This reports the spatial localization of VC EVTs, supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: HLA-G positive cells in the smooth chorion remained in the epithelial layer.

claims.evidence: This reports the spatial localization of SC EVTs, supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: EVTs were divided into clusters 1–4, with no clusters specific to the villous chorion or smooth chorion except for the small number of putative EVT Precursors.
claims.source: EVTs were further divided into clusters 1–4. No clusters were specific to the VC or SC, except for the small number of putative EVT Precursors (VC – 99 cells; SC – 8 cells) (Figure 5d, Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: This reports the results of EVT subclustering, supported by data in Figure 5d.

claims.claim: EVTs in the villous chorion have been classified as columnar, interstitial, or endovascular based on gene expression and location in the decidua.
claims.source: Previous work has classified EVTs in the VC as columnar, interstitial, or endovascular based on gene expression and location in the decidua (Tilburgs et al., 2015; Knöfler et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a citation of previous studies that classified EVT subtypes.

claims.claim: The columnar EVT subpopulation is believed to represent newly differentiated EVTs at the base of the columns connecting anchoring villi to the uterine wall.
claims.source: The columnar subpopulation is believed to represent newly differentiated EVTs, which lie at the base of the columns that connect the anchoring villi to the uterine wall.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about columnar EVTs, supported by general knowledge of placental anatomy.

claims.claim: Interstitial EVTs migrate through the decidua homing to maternal arteries, which they invade.
claims.source: Interstitial EVTs migrate through the decidua homing to maternal arteries, which they invade.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about interstitial EVTs, supported by general knowledge of placental biology.

claims.claim: The relationship between interstitial EVTs and endovascular EVTs is unclear, with evidence supporting endovascular EVTs arising either from interstitial EVTs and/or an independent origin.
claims.source: The relationship between this subpopulation and endovascular EVTs that replace the maternal arterial endothelium is unclear, with evidence supporting endovascular EVTs arising either from interstitial EVTs and/or an independent origin (Harris et al., 2009; Red-Horse et al., 2004; Pijnenborg et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about uncertainty in the field regarding EVT lineage relationships, supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Both the villous chorion and smooth chorion regions contained cells from all EVT clusters, although distinct regional biases were evident.
claims.source: We investigated the four clusters of EVT identified in our analysis in the context of the VC and the SC. Both regions contained cells from all clusters, although distinct regional biases were evident (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This reports the distribution of EVT clusters across regions, supported by data in Figure 5d and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: The smooth chorion region contained almost twice as many EVT 1 cells as the villous chorion (villous chorion – 684; smooth chorion – 1256).

claims.evidence: This reports quantitative differences in EVT cluster distribution between regions, supported by data in Figure 5d.

claims.claim: The villous chorion contained almost twice as many EVT 2–4 as the smooth chorion (villous chorion – 5789; smooth chorion – 3757).
claims.source: The SC region contained almost twice as many EVT 1 cells as the VC (VC – 684; SC – 1256), whereas the VC contained almost twice as many EVT 2–4 as the SC (VC – 5789; SC – 3757).
claims.evidence: This reports quantitative differences in EVT cluster distribution between regions, supported by data in Figure 5d.

claims.claim: Gene ontology analysis showed an enrichment for placental development and antigen presentation categories in EVT 1.
claims.source: Gene ontology analysis showed an enrichment for placental development and antigen presentation categories in EVT 1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: This reports the results of gene ontology analysis for EVT 1, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claims.claim: Representative marker genes for placental development and antigen presentation categories in EVT 1 included several lineage-specific transcription factors including GCM1, PPARG, and CEBPB.
claims.source: Representative marker genes for these categories in EVT 1 included several lineage-specific transcription factors including GCM1, PPARG, and CEBPB (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b; Knöfler et al., 2019; Ferreira et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This reports marker genes for EVT 1, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and cited references.

claims.claim: EVT 2–4 showed enrichment for extracellular structure and matrix organization, glycosylation, and peptidase activity.

claims.evidence: This reports gene expression patterns in EVT 3–4, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claims.claim: Based on gene ontology and specific gene enrichments, EVT 1 appeared most similar to columnar EVTs, while EVT 2–4 were consistent with interstitial EVTs that gain invasive capacity.
claims.source: Based on the GO and specific gene enrichments, EVT 1 appeared most similar to columnar EVTs, while EVT 2–4 were consistent with interstitial EVTs that gain invasive capacity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the gene ontology and gene expression data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The relative enrichment for EVT 1 in the smooth chorion (villous chorion – 10.57% of EVT; smooth chorion – 25.05% of EVT) suggested an expansion in columnar-like EVTs at the expense of interstitial EVT.
claims.source: The relative enrichment for EVT 1 in the SC (VC – 10.57% of EVT; SC – 25.05% of EVT) suggested an expansion in columnar-like EVTs at the expense of interstitial EVT.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the quantitative differences in EVT cluster proportions between regions.

claims.claim: The relative enrichment for EVT 2–4 in the villous chorion region suggested an expansion of the invasive subpopulation.
claims.source: Conversely, the relative enrichment for EVT 2–4 in the VC region suggested an expansion of the invasive subpopulation (Figure 5d).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the quantitative differences in EVT cluster proportions between regions.

claims.claim: Differential expression analysis between interstitial EVTs from the villous chorion and smooth chorion identified relatively few differentially expressed genes, with the vast majority having a log fold change less than 1.
claims.source: As almost 75% of EVTs from the SC region were in EVT clusters 2–4, we next asked if there were differences in gene expression between interstitial EVTs isolated from each region. claims.evidence: This reports the results of differential expression analysis between regions for EVT 2–4, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2a.

claims.claim: The small number of differentially expressed genes with a fold change greater than 1 between villous chorion and smooth chorion EVTs was typically identified across multiple EVT clusters.

claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the differential expression analysis results.

claims.claim: Differential expression analysis of all EVT subclusters combined revealed the hormone CSH1 and several proteases including HTRA1, HTRA4, and PAPPA to be expressed at significantly higher levels in the more invasive villous chorion EVTs.

results.result: The study used single-cell RNA-sequencing to profile cells from the villous chorion (VC) and smooth chorion (SC) of four second-trimester human placentas (gestational weeks 17.6-24.0). After quality control, 50,496 cells were analyzed, with cells from both regions well-represented and enriched for cytotrophoblasts (CTBs) as expected from the enrichment protocol.
results.evaluation: The experimental design and data collection are well-documented with appropriate sample sizes (n=4 placentas, 8 datasets), clear dissection protocols, and standard quality control metrics. The use of 10× Genomics platform and computational integration methods are appropriate and properly cited. Cell type annotations using canonical markers are validated against published datasets.

results.result: A novel CTB population termed SC-specific CTBs (SC-CTBs or CTB 4) was identified exclusively in the smooth chorion, marked by expression of region-specific cytokeratins (KRT6A, KRT14, KRT17). SC-CTBs comprise 20.8% of CTBs in the SC but are absent from the VC, forming a stratified epithelium above a basal layer of progenitor CTBs (CTB 1).
results.evaluation: The identification of SC-CTBs is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence: scRNA-seq data showing distinct clustering (Figure 2), marker gene expression (KRT6A, KRT14, KRT17), immunofluorescence validation showing spatial organization (Figure 2h-i), and independent clustering confirming region-specificity. The quantification is consistent across samples, and integration with published datasets confirms novelty.

results.result: RNA velocity analysis revealed that CTB 1 progenitors in the VC differentiate into syncytiotrophoblasts (STBs) by upregulating syncytialization factors (ERVW-1, ERVFRD-1, GCM1), while CTB 1 progenitors in the SC take an alternative trajectory toward SC-CTBs (CTB 2-4) by upregulating epithelial transcription factors (KLF4, YAP1, HES1) instead.
results.evaluation: The lineage trajectories are well-supported by RNA velocity analysis (Figure 3a-b), pseudotime modeling (Figure 3c), and differential gene expression patterns. The VC trajectory recapitulates established knowledge of STB differentiation, while the SC trajectory is novel and supported by uniform directionality in velocity vectors. The absence of STB differentiation markers in SC CTBs and presence of proliferating KRT6+ cells further support the alternative trajectory.

results.result: SC-CTBs express epidermal and metabolic transcriptional programs consistent with barrier function and pathogen defense. Gene ontology analysis revealed enrichment for cell junction organization, skin/epidermal development, and antiviral response genes. SC-CTBs show progressive cytokeratin expression (KRT7/8/18 → KRT14/17 → KRT6A) and express IFITM3, an antiviral restriction factor.
results.evaluation: The functional characterization is well-supported by gene ontology analysis (Figure 4a), marker gene expression validated by immunofluorescence (Figure 4b-e), and comparison to epidermal tissues. The progressive cytokeratin expression pattern is documented across differentiation stages. However, the functional claims are largely inferential based on gene expression patterns rather than direct functional assays. The speculation about IFITM3 blocking STB differentiation (C140-C141) is appropriately labeled as such.

results.result: EVTs from the VC and SC are transcriptionally similar despite distinct invasive behaviors in vivo. Both regions contain EVT clusters 1-4, but the SC shows enrichment for columnar-like EVT 1 (25.05% vs 10.57% in VC), while the VC shows enrichment for invasive EVT 2-4. Differential expression analysis revealed few genes with fold change >1, with CSH1 being the most differentially expressed and exclusive to VC EVTs.
results.evaluation: The transcriptional similarity of EVTs between regions is well-documented through multiple analyses: correlation coefficients (Figure 5—figure supplement 2c), permutation-based differential expression showing EVTs have the lowest number of differentially expressed genes (Figure 5g), and gene ontology analysis. The quantitative differences in EVT cluster proportions are consistent across samples. However, the functional interpretation that differences are primarily non-cell autonomous (C171, C174) is inferential and requires further validation.

results.result: SC-CTBs physically associate with EVTs in the SC epithelium and secrete factors that inhibit EVT invasion. Immunofluorescence showed widespread KRT6+/HLA-G+ cell contacts in the SC but not VC. Transwell invasion assays demonstrated that SC conditioned medium significantly reduced VC cell invasion (p<0.01) without affecting cell density, while VC conditioned medium had no effect. CellPhoneDB analysis identified multiple predicted secreted factors from CTB 4 to EVTs including TNFα, PGF, TGFB1, FGF1, PDGFB, FN1, and THBS1.
results.evaluation: The physical association is well-documented by immunofluorescence (Figure 6a-b). The functional inhibition is demonstrated by transwell assays with appropriate controls (n=3 biological replicates, conditioned media from 3 placentas) showing significant reduction in invasion (Figure 6c-d). Cell density measurements confirm the effect is on invasion rather than proliferation/survival. The inference that SC-CTBs produce the inhibitory factors (C191) is reasonable given they are unique to the SC, but the specific factors remain to be validated. The CellPhoneDB predictions (C192) are computational and require experimental validation.

results.result: The study identified and characterized immune and stromal cell populations in both regions. Immune cells (14,805 total) were of maternal origin based on XIST expression, with the VC showing higher proportions of macrophages and the SC showing higher proportions of NK/T cells. Stromal cells (3,883 total) included two SC-specific fetal mesenchymal populations (Mesenchyme 1 and 3) marked by COL11A1 expression. Both regions showed expression of CTB support factors (HGF, WNT2, RSPO3) in fetal stromal populations.
results.evaluation: The immune and stromal characterization is supported by appropriate clustering, marker gene expression, XIST-based origin determination, and validation against published datasets (Vento-Tormo et al., 2018; Pique-Regi et al., 2019). However, the authors acknowledge that differences in immune cell proportions may be artifacts of dissection/enrichment protocol (C58), and stromal analysis is limited by depletion during CTB enrichment. The findings are appropriately presented as descriptive rather than mechanistic.

results.result: Two cycling CTB populations (S-phase and G2/M-phase) were identified based on expression of phasic transcripts (MKI67, PCNA, TOP2A). These cycling cells share gene expression with all CTB clusters but lack STB and EVT markers, consistent with the requirement for cell cycle exit upon terminal differentiation. Cycling CTBs comprise similar proportions in both regions (22.1% VC, 17.5% SC).
results.evaluation: The identification of cycling populations is well-supported by canonical cell cycle marker expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b), shared gene expression with CTB clusters, and absence of differentiation markers consistent with established biology. The similar proportions across regions suggest comparable proliferative capacity. This is a standard finding in scRNA-seq studies and appropriately characterized.

results.result: CellPhoneDB analysis identified region-specific signaling interactions. In the SC, BMP, Notch, and Ephrin signaling events were specific to CTB-CTB interactions. For EVT-stromal interactions, the VC showed enrichment for collagen-integrin interactions while the SC showed PDGFA and FN1 signaling. These differential signaling patterns may create stromal environments with different invasive capacities.
results.evaluation: The CellPhoneDB predictions are computational and based on co-expression of ligand-receptor pairs. While the analysis is appropriately conducted and cited, these are predictions that require experimental validation. The authors acknowledge that stromal analysis is limited by depletion during enrichment. The model that differential signaling creates different stromal environments (C174) is speculative and not directly tested. The predictions provide hypotheses for future work but are not experimentally validated in this study.

results.result: The introduction establishes the anatomical structure of the human placenta, the limited understanding of SC cellular composition, and the rationale for using scRNA-seq at mid-gestation. Previous studies at term recovered very few CTBs from the SC (0.44% in Pique-Regi et al., 2019), potentially reflecting difficulty in capturing these cells at term.
results.evaluation: The background information is well-supported by appropriate citations to established literature. The anatomical descriptions are accurate and the gap in knowledge is clearly articulated. The citation of previous scRNA-seq studies and their limitations provides appropriate context for the current study. The speculation about difficulty capturing term CTBs (C36) is appropriately presented as such.

results.result: CTB 2 and CTB 3 represent intermediate states in SC-CTB differentiation with distinct functional signatures. CTB 2 highly expresses CLU, CFD, and IFIT3, suggesting roles in innate immune response to bacterial/viral infection. CTB 3 upregulates EGLN3 and SLC2A3, indicating HIF-mediated hypoxia response and glucose metabolism adaptation.
results.evaluation: The identification of intermediate states is supported by transcriptional similarity analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c), RNA velocity showing progression (Figure 3b), and pseudotime modeling (Figure 3c). The marker gene expression is documented, and functional inferences are appropriately based on known gene functions with citations. However, these are inferential functional assignments based on gene expression rather than direct functional assays.

results.result: EVT clusters were characterized and related to known EVT subtypes. EVT 1 showed enrichment for placental development and antigen presentation genes (GCM1, PPARG, CEBPB), consistent with columnar EVTs. EVT 2-4 showed enrichment for extracellular matrix organization and proteases (HTRA1, MMP2, MMP11), consistent with invasive interstitial EVTs.
results.evaluation: The EVT characterization is supported by gene ontology analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and marker gene expression. The assignment to known EVT subtypes (columnar vs interstitial) is inferential based on gene expression patterns and comparison to literature, which is appropriate. However, the authors acknowledge uncertainty about the relationship between interstitial and endovascular EVTs (C154), appropriately citing conflicting evidence in the literature.
